messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 24
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: QA Engineer
- Trauma Type: Man-made disaster
- Pcl5: 56

At 24, he works as a QA engineer for a midsize software company, the kind of job he once liked for its orderliness. He spends his days trying to break things on purpose so other people do not have to. Before the trauma, that logic comforts him. He likes test cases, reproducible errors, the relief of finding the flaw before it reaches production. He is single, lives alone, calls his mother most Sundays, and describes himself as someone who has always preferred predictability.

The event that divides his life into before and after happens a little over a year ago, during what is supposed to be an ordinary evening in the city. He has stayed late at the office to help verify a release. When he finally leaves, he stops at a crowded transit terminal to catch a bus home. He remembers checking his phone, half-reading work messages, half-thinking about what to eat for dinner. Then there is a sudden blast from across the terminal—violent, metallic, unreal at first, followed by screaming and the sharp smell of smoke and something chemical he still cannot name without feeling sick. For a few seconds he does not understand what has happened. He sees glass on the ground, people falling, someone grabbing his arm and then disappearing in the surge.

What he remembers most clearly is not a single image but fragments: a woman crying for her son, a shoe without a foot in it, the fire alarm strobing red over the crowd. He drops to the ground because someone else does, then runs because everyone runs. He tells himself later that he should have helped more, should have gone back, should have done something other than save himself. At the time, he is moving on pure instinct, heart pounding so hard it hurts, lungs burning as he reaches the street. He spends hours that night trying to contact family so they do not see the news first and think he is dead. He does not sleep. Every time he closes his eyes, the blast happens again.

In the first weeks after, he goes back to work quickly, almost defiantly. He tells coworkers he is lucky, that he is fine, that other people had it worse. But his body does not believe him. The hiss of the office espresso machine makes him flinch. When a developer slams a conference room door, he feels the shock in his chest before he can think. During testing, if an application freezes or a system alert suddenly sounds, he startles so visibly that people laugh awkwardly and then pretend not to notice. He begins wearing headphones all day, not for music but to blunt the world.

Sleep becomes uneven and thin. Some nights he avoids bed until two or three in the morning because he dreads the dreams. In them he is back in the terminal, except each time the details shift: sometimes he cannot run, sometimes he is searching through smoke for someone he has never met, sometimes he looks down and finds blood on his own shirt. He wakes soaked in sweat, checks the locks, checks the windows, and sits on the edge of the bed waiting for his pulse to slow.

He starts arranging his life around avoidance. He no longer takes public transit and pays for rides he cannot really afford. He skips a friend’s birthday because it is in a busy bar near downtown. He stands near exits in restaurants, scans strangers’ hands and backpacks, notices security cameras and blocked doorways before he notices faces. His mother tells him he sounds far away on the phone. He calls less often after that, ashamed of how little patience he has. When she asks what is wrong, he says work is stressful.

At work, the parts of him that used to feel competent are harder to access. He rereads bug reports three times and still misses details. He opens a test plan and suddenly sees the terminal floor instead of the screen. When deadlines pile up, he becomes irritable in ways that embarrass him. A teammate asks an ordinary question during stand-up, and he snaps back too sharply, then spends the rest of the day replaying it. He has always been careful and thorough; now he doubts himself constantly. His job depends on anticipating failure, and lately his mind does that everywhere, with everyone, all the time.

He does not talk much about the guilt unless he has been sitting in the room for a while. Then he says he keeps thinking about the people who did not make it out, and about the injured man he saw near the platform but did not stop for. He knows, rationally, that he was terrified and disoriented. He says this like he is reciting a fact from someone else’s case. Emotionally, he still believes he failed some test of character in the worst moment of his life.

Now, in the present, his world has narrowed without his meaning for it to. He goes to work, comes home, orders food, watches the same shows he barely follows, and checks breaking news compulsively for any sign of another attack. Crowds exhaust him. Sudden noises send a jolt through him. He feels older than 24, but also strangely suspended at the age he was that evening, as if some part of him never fully left the station. Even on quieter days, he moves through life braced for impact, waiting for danger to announce itself again.
